claims.text: Incorporating graphene nanoplatelets during high-entropy-alloy processing will form a durable self-lubricating tribolayer.
The graphene-derived tribolayer will lower the coefficient of friction.
The graphene-derived tribolayer will lower the wear rate.
The untreated high-entropy alloy has a conventional microstructure without integrated lubricious phases.
Graphene nanoplatelets can be uniformly dispersed throughout the alloy matrix during consolidation.
The intervention should remain effective from room temperature to approximately 600°C in non-corrosive atmospheres.
Sliding mechanically exposes dispersed graphene nanoplatelets at the contact interface.
Mechanically exposed graphene nanoplatelets form a continuous lubricious tribolayer.
Mechanical stress aligns the graphene nanoplatelets to form a sliding interface.
Alignment of graphene nanoplatelets reduces interfacial shear resistance.
The low shear strength of the graphene layer lowers friction.
The stability of the graphene layer lowers wear.
The graphene tribolayer is sufficiently resilient to sustain its lubricating effect throughout the specified temperature range.
The graphene-enhanced alloy will exhibit at least a 20–30% reduction in coefficient of friction relative to the untreated alloy.
The graphene-enhanced alloy will exhibit at least a 20–30% reduction in wear rate relative to the untreated alloy.
Aggressive corrosive species may diminish the lubricating effect by disrupting the tribolayer.
Temperatures beyond graphene's stability range may disrupt the tribolayer and diminish lubrication.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified alloy fails to reduce both friction and wear by at least 20–30% relative to the untreated control, or if no tribolayer is detected.
